title: Could a Stick of Gum Replace Anxiety Meds? These Teens Are Chewing on It
summary: Imagine if the cure for pre-test jitters or social anxiety was already in your pocket — in a stick of gum. That's the future Zackary Nizker and Sara Hoti, both 16, are working toward. The McIntosh High School juniors have developed a prototype chewing gum that delivers flavonoids, natural anti-anxiety compounds found in passionflower (Passiflora incarnata). Their project earned them fourth place and $600 at the 2026 Regeneron International Science & Engineering Fair (ISEF), a global competition that drew 1,725 finalists from 65 countries. The idea is personal for Zackary. "A third of all adolescents and young adults suffer from a form of anxiety," he says, citing U.S. data. His grandmother's severe anxiety and the debilitating side effects of her prescription drugs — "she could hardly walk or stand" — drove him to seek a gentler alternative. Passionflower, which grows wild in their hometown of Peachtree City, Georgia, has been studied for decades. Its flavonoids boost levels of GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid), a neurotransmitter that slows neuron firing and calms an overactive brain. "Chewing gum, by itself, is already known to reduce anxiety," Zackary notes. Combining rhythmic chewing with passionflower extract, they hypothesized, could create a more effective, on-the-go treatment. But first they had to prove their gum could deliver a consistent dose. They cooked up bubble gum using a gum base, powdered sugar, sweeteners, and purchased passionflower extract (the flowers were out of season). Then came the tricky part: testing without human subjects. "We're not allowed to just give people some random gum we made," Zackary says. So they turned to two in vitro methods. Under a microscope, they analyzed slices of gum to measure flavonoid particle distribution. A value below 15 indicates uniformity; theirs scored 8.4 — "perfect," Sara says. The second test, the Shinoda test, checks flavonoid stability. Normally used for liquids, adapting it for solid gum was a "really long process," Sara admits. They soaked gum pieces in alcohol to simulate saliva, but the flavonoids stubbornly stayed put. That's promising: it suggests the gum could release the compounds gradually during chewing, rather than all at once. The next phase? Clinical trials to see if the gum actually reduces anxiety in people. If it works, a simple chew could become a discreet, accessible tool for millions of teens — and adults like Zackary's grandmother — seeking calm without harsh side effects.
why_it_matters: If a cheap, accessible chewing gum can genuinely ease anxiety, it could reshape how millions of young people — and adults — cope with daily stress, offering a tool that fits in a pocket instead of a prescription bottle with scary side effects.

background_read: Passionflower (Passiflora incarnata), a vine native to the southeastern United States, has been used for centuries by Native American tribes to soothe nerves and aid sleep. Its calming effect is now known to come from flavonoids that raise levels of GABA, the brain’s main off-switch chemical, which was first discovered in the 1950s.

Prescription anti-anxiety medications like benzodiazepines can cause side effects including drowsiness, dizziness, and difficulty with coordination; many patients, like Zackary’s grandmother, struggle to function while taking them.

The Regeneron International Science & Engineering Fair (ISEF) is the world’s largest pre-college science competition, run by the Society for Science. Since 1950, it has showcased projects by teenage researchers who often go on to major discoveries. Zackary and Sara’s work follows in the footsteps of past ISEF finalists who have tackled health problems with natural molecules.

Chewing gum itself has been shown in small studies to lower cortisol (the stress hormone) and increase alertness, but combining it with an active botanical ingredient was a new twist that required inventing test methods no one had used on solid gum before.

perspectives.description: For teenagers who feel the pressure of school, social media, and future uncertainty, a safe, natural alternative to medication could make mental health support as simple as chewing gum. It would reduce stigma and give people a sense of control without numbing side effects. Zackary’s grandmother represents millions who could regain daily function without being incapacitated by their treatment.

Skeptics worry that a gum might not deliver a strong enough dose for serious anxiety and could discourage people from seeking professional therapy or proper medication when needed. Adapting lab tests for gum was difficult, and proving it works in real brains — not just in a dish — is a huge leap. Without rigorous clinical evidence, the risk is a trendy product that overpromises.

The project sits at the intersection of ethnobotany, neuroscience, and materials science: it takes an ancient plant remedy and modern drug-delivery thinking. The challenge of creating a stable, uniform solid dose mirrors problems in the pharmaceutical industry. Their use of in vitro methods to simulate chewing shows how teen scientists can innovate tests when human trials aren’t yet possible — a model for early-stage research.

If clinical trials succeed, the gum could be licensed by a health company and sold over the counter, much like nicotine gum. School counselors might recommend it for test anxiety, and airports could stock it for nervous flyers. The real breakthrough might be paving the way for other flavonoid-based edible products that deliver brain-calming nutrients through everyday items like mints or tea.
